newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - HK migrants seek gold streets, find struggle.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - HK migrants seek gold streets, find struggle.

text.p: They come seeking fortune from mainland China's Third World economy to Hong Kong's glittering First World riches. Adjusting to change is a tough problem for new settlers in one of the world's most competitive societies.
Daily, 150 legal immigrants, including children and pregnant women, cross into this East Asian economic hub, with such dreams that they almost expect to find streets paved with gold.
These are the lucky ones, but even then many face poverty, a struggle to get housing and jobs while their children, equipped with scant knowledge of English, battle to adapt at school.

Scores of others, illegal immigrants, risk their lives in hazardous border crossings by land or sea. Those caught are swiftly returned. The border remains tightly guarded even though Hong Kong has been a special region of China since July 1.
Children from separated families seeking to rejoin a parent in Hong Kong are sneaked in by smugglers running a lucrative trade in human cargoes past frontier checkpoints.
But controversially Hong Kong, a crowded metropolis of 6.4 million people, plans to deport hundreds or thousands of these youngsters to deter "queue-jumping."
LEGAL MIGRANTS NOW DOUBLE, MORE EXPECTED
The annual intake of legal migrants nearly doubled in two years to 61,000 in 1996, and the pressure is on for a big spurt in numbers now that Hong Kong is a special Chinese region.
China, with 1.2 billion people and the world's largest nation, lags at least 20 years behind its "Pearl of the Orient" region, among the most prosperous cities anywhere.
For newly arrived mainland children it's sink-or-swim in adapting to a modern and international city, but educators praise their struggle to catch up.

"The difficulties for them are mostly adaptation to the new environment in classrooms, and the obvious difficulty is English," said Chan Tak Hang, deputy headmaster of Pui Ching Middle Shool which uses Chinese as the medium of instruction.

"Every year, we recruit about 30 mainland students who have been in Hong Kong not more than two years, (so) we don't face much pressure and difficulties in teaching. Our students are qualified to catch up to the English standard here in a short time," Chan said.
Chan believes mainland students here are especially good in Chinese language and mathematics.

"Their Chinese is much better than Hong Kong students', and they can communicate in Mandarin; the standard of mathematics in the mainland is higher than in Hong Kong, so these students do better than Hong Kong students," he said.
MAINLAND STUDENTS SEEN BETTER EXCEPT FOR ENGLISH
Except for English, senior mainland students generally have a deeper knowledge in subjects and so can compete effectively.
"Lessons taught in villages and cities are very different. Our students are mostly from cities, so they face fewer difficulties in adapting their lives in Hong Kong," Chan said.
Another Chinese teaching school, Heung To Middle School, recruits 100 to 150 mainland students every year in pre-high school classes for students 12 to 16 years old.
Ho Ping Kuen, chief of the school's education department, said that students are mostly weak only in English. "Many need a long time to catch up because of poor English," he said.
Change of environment was a difficulty too. Many from once-divided families were poor and had to learn to live with fathers they had rarely seen before they came to Hong Kong.
"Most of their fathers are less educated and aged, so they have to cope with a strange human," he said.
Hong Kong's Education Department, together with voluntary organisations, offer English remedial courses and adjustment programmes in some districts.
Mainland youngsters can also qualify for psychological therapy services.
